title: Meta wants to pay for its broad AI buildout with a newly created class of stock
description: The social media giant is planning a new stock strategy to help power its broad investments in AI models and services.
content: Meta is making a big push into AI, and it’s creating a new kind of stock that could help pay for it. On Wednesday, as the company reported its third-quarter earnings, Semafor reported the company might issue non-voting stock, meaning shares that don’t give their owners a vote on company decisions, to help fund its push into artificial intelligence. During Meta’s earnings call, the company confirmed that reporting. Meta’s chief financial officer, Susan Li, said the company plans to “create a new class of non-voting capital stock, which will be distributed to all existing shareholders through a stock dividend.” Li later added that the company “created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, and other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders.” The shares will allow the company to maintain its current “founder-led structure,” she added. They will also expand its “funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business, driven by AI.” Meta’s earnings were strong this past quarter, beating Wall Street expectations. The company made $64 billion in revenue, a jump of 26% from a year earlier. Its costs and expenses also rose, however, by 68% year-over-year. Reality Labs, the division responsible for Meta’s AR glasses, VR headsets, and VR software, continues to lose money, though less than it used to. The company said in its earnings report that it expects the division’s losses to shrink from its 2025 levels to between $18 billion and $19 billion. Meta has made a big push into AI over the past year. The company has released several AI models, including Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer earlier this year. In recent weeks, it added Muse Wonder and Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model whose underlying parameters are publicly available for outsiders to use and build on. Meta also launched a coding agent for software developers called Muse Code. At its Meta Connect event this year, the company announced a new line of cute and cuddly avatars for AI assistant, Meta Muse, in a push to make its AI services more relatable (and also meme-able ). As far as can be discerned, those AI products are doing well. “In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada have set up Muse personal agents,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during Wednesday’s earnings call. “Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number one in the App Store almost every day.” “Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg added, claiming later that the company expects to grow the product’s appeal to eventually “serve billions of people.” The company also noted that certain storm clouds linger on the horizon in the form of ongoing regulatory and legal issues. “We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” said Li. “For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets, and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States.” Topics AI , Facebook , Mark Zuckerberg , Meta , muse , Social When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Back to Articles a]:hidden"> NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required Enterprise + Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 31 +25 Joshua Przybylko jprzybylko Follow nvidia Valter Hudovernik valterh-nv Follow nvidia Federico Lopez flopeznv Follow nvidia Akihiro Nitta akihironitta-nv Follow nvidia Ramona Bendias RBendiasN Follow nvidia Ardrian Wong aw777 Follow nvidia Jure Leskovec profjure Follow nvidia Matthias Fey rusty1s Follow nvidia :last-child]:mb-0"> TL;DR NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers historical examples as context examples and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models and kumo-engine libraries, or as an NVIDIA NIM. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596 Model Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models Model Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational Client Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client NIM Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications. The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons: Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational. Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization. Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions. Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational ( Paper , GitHub , HuggingFace ), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required. How Kumo Relational Works Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation ( e.g. , "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort. Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning by reasoning over context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target ( e.g. , "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units"). Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference. To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works: Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables. Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL) , a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage. Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently via column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates. Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, followed by cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs. How Kumo Relational Was Built Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures. The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited. Pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases. Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. Performance In the paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. It is the top-performing in-context learning model on the RelBench leaderboard . On RelArena-α , it sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front: Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard as of 2026-09-21: Elo across tasks versus total task runtime (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than rtl-plurel at similar accuracy. On the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when noisy columns are added. Limitations Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions. Predictive signals must be reachable within a limited number of hops. Demo Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory , through database and warehouse connectors , or through kumo-engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. The model itself is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular . The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The interface is designed to naturally extend tabular foundation models to relational signal by passing additional related multi-table context and query information: import sdm # pip install structured-data-models model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device= "cuda" ) pred = model( # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets): x_context=sdm.TableTensor(...), y_context=sdm.TableTensor(...), # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps): x_query=sdm.TableTensor(...), # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities: related_context_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}), related_query_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}), ) See the library's relational examples for RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines. To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request: import sdm_client # pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]' client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url= "http://localhost:8001" ) # NIM URL query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery( # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL): "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id" , # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred): { "users" : ..., "orders" : ...}, ) pred = client.predict( # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict: query.materialize(indices=[ 1 , 2 , 3 ]), model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(), ) See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks. title: PHP Armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
description: This is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented by AI, but is also a high risk because of AI.
content: The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation . PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites . It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress. The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app. Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12. So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz. Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post . Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP. Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help. Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.) OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws. In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI. Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can. title: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
description: As Amazon blocks AI agents from shopping on its site, Walmart is taking the opposite approach, introducing new technology that lets AI agents make purchases on customers' behalf, with controls over spending and transaction approvals.
content: Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers. The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. Now it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart president and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club. It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do. With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified and you can cap their spending. The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site. title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium. Enterprise Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 11 +5 Josh Longenecker jlongen-aws Follow amazon :last-child]:mb-0"> Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent. This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron , its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile , and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know: How to configure torch.profiler with the Neuron backend and capture a clean trace. How to read the key_averages() table to identify which operations consume Neuron device time and compare their Self CPU time. How to follow one operation through Neuron Explorer, from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution on a NeuronCore. How these signals change across three implementations of the same operation. Neuron as a PyTorch Backend Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch. The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda . The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1 . Set Up the Profiler You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload: NeuronConfig controls which Neuron data streams and NeuronCores to capture and where to write the output. You pass it to torch.profiler.profile as experimental_config . NeuronProfiler takes a NeuronConfig and provides an export_trace callback. The callback writes the framework trace, trace.json , alongside the Neuron system traces. nc = NeuronConfig( modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME], profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR, capture_enabled_for_nc= '0' , correlate_device_time= True , ) exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc) The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation . Tooling: Neuron Explorer Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches. After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions. Profile RMSNorm For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations. You profile three implementations of the same operation: Naive RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations: multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply. torch.rms_norm() , the PyTorch built-in lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel. Naive RMSNorm with torch.compile , using the same operations as the first implementation. The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable. All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory . Profile 1: Naive PyTorch Operations Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors. device = torch.device( 'neuron' ) x = torch.randn( 4 , 512 , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device) weight = torch.ones( 512 , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device) def rms_norm_fn ( t ): x_sq = t * t # square mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=- 1 , keepdim= True ) # mean of squares rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6 ) # 1 / sqrt(mean_sq + eps) return t * rms * weight # normalize + scale Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend: Include ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1 to collect activity from the Neuron device. Pass NeuronConfig as experimental_config to enable the Neuron-specific Kineto features. The schedule uses wait=2 , warmup=1 , and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead. Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty. with torch.profiler.profile( activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1], experimental_config=nc, record_shapes= False , on_trace_ready=exporter.export_trace, schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait= 2 , warmup= 1 , active= 1 ), ) as prof: for step in range ( 4 ): with torch.no_grad(): _ = rms_norm_fn(x) torch.neuron.synchronize() prof.step() After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers. print (prof.key_averages().table(sort_by= "self_privateuse1_time_total" , row_limit= 4 )) The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time. The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications. Name # Calls Self CPU Self NEURON % NEURON aten::mul 3 60.9 μs 1,164.5 μs 49.5% aten::add 1 26.6 μs 434.6 μs 18.5% aten::rsqrt 1 15.6 μs 415.0 μs 17.6% aten::mean 1 21.1 μs 340.8 μs 14.5% Self NEURON total: 2.355 ms Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x , x * rms , and the final multiplication by weight . aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root. Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes. Read the Trace in Explorer In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule , and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running . The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier: Lane Label suffix What it shows Framework dispatch framework/TID:<id> Operator dispatch events (PrivateUse1 runtime), grouped by thread ID. Framework device framework/Stream:<n> Device interaction events (PrivateUse1 driver), grouped by stream number. Neuron Runtime neuron_rt/NC:<n> Neuron Runtime API calls, grouped by logical NeuronCore. Neuron Hardware neuron_hw/NC<n>:<id> Hardware execution events, grouped by physical NeuronCore. In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution. The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes. Profile 2: torch.rms_norm Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel: def rms_norm_fn ( t ): return torch.rms_norm(t, [ 512 ], weight) The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table. Name # Calls Self CPU Self NEURON % NEURON aten::_fused_rms_norm 1 47.6 μs 403.3 μs 100% Self NEURON total: 403.3 μs The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately. Compare the Lowering Path In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations. Profile 3: Naive PyTorch with torch.compile For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile . With @torch.compile(backend="neuron") , TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch. @torch.compile( backend= 'neuron' , fullgraph= True ) def naive_compiled ( t ): x_sq = t * t mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=- 1 , keepdim= True ) rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6 ) return t * rms * weight The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table. Name # Calls Self CPU Self NEURON % NEURON Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0 1 98.4 μs 375.5 μs 100% Self NEURON total: 375.5 μs The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution. The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm , at 375 μs compared with 403 μs. Side-by-Side Summary Variant NEURON time Self CPU time Operator calls Naive ops 2,355 µs ~125 µs 6 torch.rms_norm 403 µs ~48 µs 1 Naive + torch.compile 376 µs ~98 µs 1 Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations. Conclusion key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes. You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost. In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound. Agents also can only access information needed to complete their task. Walmart says it will block agents that don’t follow these terms. Your AI agent will get its own profile within your Walmart account. Image: Walmart Related Websites are closing their doors to AI agents Agents will connect to new “Agent Profiles” within Walmart. By default, Walmart will require approval for all AI agent purchases, but you can also let it shop within a certain budget, such as up to $100. You’ll also be able to review your agent’s purchases separately from your own in Agent Profiles, as well as turn off the agent at any time. The retailer has built an “Agent Gateway,” currently available in beta , that connects AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that allows AI agents to plug into different services on the web. Walmart says this not only enables AI agents to shop without running into hiccups that they might encounter when navigating a browser, but also prevents them from accessing your shopping history and personal information. “For example, if a customer tends to buy sourdough bread or a particular brand of milk, Walmart will help the agent find those usual items for the customer without sharing the customer’s broader shopping history with the agent,” Walmart says. The company will let users shop with AI agents on Sam’s Club as well. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. description: Meta Muse users are adopting the app for shopping and personal productivity, the company said during its Q3 earnings call. The AI app now has over 10M users.
content: Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention. He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders. “Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping. Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content. Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said. Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay. Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales. “On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.” Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year. Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].” “And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added. title: Announcing SimReady Central: An Open Library of Simulation-Ready 3D Assets for Robotics and AI Factories
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Announcing SimReady Central: An Open Library of Simulation-Ready 3D Assets for Robotics and AI Factories Enterprise + Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote - John Kosnik jkosnik Follow nvidia Frank DeLise delisef Follow nvidia Pomi Lee pomilee Follow nvidia :last-child]:mb-0"> Building robotics simulations and high-fidelity AI factory digital twins takes more than 3D models. Developers often need to add properties such as collision geometry, mass, and friction. SimReady assets are 3D models that come prepared with the properties required for simulation workflows, reducing that manual work. SimReady Central Library brings together more than 2,000 simulation-ready (SimReady) OpenUSD assets on Hugging Face, giving developers a free, ungated starting point for physical AI training environments and AI factory digital twins. The library includes a variety of infrastructure and equipment assets from robot arms and grippers to warehouse equipment, racks, and cooling infrastructure. Developers can check which capabilities each asset supports, then combine assets from different suppliers into a scene. Equipment manufacturers (OEMs) can now prepare and validate assets against SimReady requirements and use SimReady Central Library to reach developers and allow their end customers to test and simulate scenarios faster and accelerate decision making. This enables industries to build simulations around their products while managing their own Hugging Face datasets. We’ll cover what makes an asset SimReady and how OEMs contribute to SimReady Central Library, then show how developers can use those assets to build a robotic pick-and-place scenario and compare AI factory layouts . What makes an asset SimReady? SimReady assets are OpenUSD assets prepared with the properties required for simulation workflows. A detailed 3D model, such as CAD, is a useful starting point. Simulation requires additional information about how that object should be interpreted and used. For a robot manipulation task, that might include the object’s mass, collision geometry, and friction properties. For AI factory workflows, it might include equipment geometry and the electrical or thermal metadata required by the application. OpenUSD is an open, extensible framework for describing and composing 3D scenes. Using those scenes to train and evaluate autonomous machines also requires information about physical behavior, collisions, and sensor interactions. SimReady Foundation provides specifications, profiles, and validation tools that make these requirements explicit. A profile defines the logical grouping of features and capabilities an asset needs for a particular use case. Figure 1. SimReady Foundation defines asset representation requirements for specific simulation use cases, while developer libraries help prepare and validate OpenUSD assets against those requirements. Depending on the asset and profile, those features can include: Asset structural elements What it enables Collision geometry and physical properties Contact and physics simulation in a supported runtime. Joint structure and limits Articulated robot and equipment movement. Semantic labels Object identification and annotated synthetic data. Materials and sensor attributes Rendering and supporting sensor simulation. For the requirements associated with each simulation use case, see the SimReady Foundation requirements and profiles . Developers should select assets from SimReady Central whose profiles match their workflow needs and compose them into an OpenUSD scene. Why publish OEM assets to SimReady Central? OEMs can turn their CAD equipment models into SimReady assets for developers building simulations around their products. SimReady Central Library makes those assets discoverable on Hugging Face, helping manufacturers reach teams building robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins. For AI factory OEMs like Vertiv , the library provides a path to distribute assets such as warehouse equipment racks, server racks, cooling equipment, and supporting infrastructure for AI factory digital twins. Developers and frontier agents can incorporate these assets into AI factory digital twins reusing the geometry and properties specified by their SimReady profiles. For robotics OEMs like Comau , FANUC , Franka Robotics , Robotiq , Standard Bots , and Universal Robots , the library makes robot arms and grippers discoverable by teams building training and evaluation environments. Developers can combine these assets with industrial equipment to build warehouse and factory scenarios. For simulation asset providers like Palatial the library features the NVIDIA Robotics 1K Dataset released in collaboration with NVIDIA Robotics, alongside complex articulated assets generated from text, images, scans, datasheets, and CAD. Developers can build assets and scenes for robot training and evaluation. For OEMs like LG Electronics (LGE) that develop robots for the home alongside the appliances they work with, the library provides a path to share assets such as refrigerators and dishwashers. Developers can use assets informed by LGE’s experience in both appliances and robotics to build household simulation environments for robot training, evaluation, and synthetic data generation. For AI-assisted CAD providers like ForgeCAD , the library makes articulated robotics props with high-quality textures available, which developers can use to build environments for robot perception and manipulation training, as well as synthetic data generation. To contribute, OEMs can use the SimReady Central submission skill to validate assets against the relevant SimReady profiles, package them, and submit them for inclusion in the library. Figure 2. OEMs prepare and validate OpenUSD assets against SimReady profiles and then submit the asset to SimReady Central. Developers and AI agents discover assets in the library and use them to build simulation environments. Build simulation environments with SimReady assets SimReady Central gives robotics and industrial developers a reusable starting point for robot workcells, industrial environments, and AI factory digital twins. Developers and AI agents can find assets in SimReady Central that meet the profiles required by their workflows and compose them into OpenUSD environments. Developers can use SimReady assets to populate training environments with objects and obstacles, then vary their placement to evaluate robot behaviors. These environments can support projects such as Microduck, an open-source robot from Hugging Face and Pollen Robotics. Figure 3. Asset datasets connect through SimReady Central on Hugging Face, using its USD search service to support Isaac workflows, SimReady Central library search, and AI agent workflows. NVIDIA USD Search powers natural-language search in SimReady Central Library, helping developers and AI agents find assets across participating datasets. Hugging Face has also integrated USD Search into their platform search with indexed USD properties and simulation metadata, helping agents discover SimReady assets suited to their physical AI simulation tasks. AI-assisted authoring adds another way to build with those assets. Developers can use frontier models like OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra combined with asset search and scene-authoring tools to build environments using SimReady Central Library. Given task requirements and spatial constraints, Astra can help find suitable assets, write code to assemble a scene, and create scenario variations. OEMs can also use Astra to help prepare and refine OpenUSD assets against SimReady Foundation requirements before validating and submitting them to the library. Build a robotic pick-and-place scenario For example, a developer building a robotic pick-and-place scenario could start with this prompt: Using SimReady assets from SimReady Central on Hugging Face, create a basic warehouse pick-and-place scenario in Isaac Sim using PhysX. Use the nvidia-simready-central.hf.space to find a FANUC robotic arm, a compatible Robotiq gripper, and suitable warehouse assets. Generate the Python code to assemble the scene and configure the pick-and-place task. Render a .mov preview so I can review the results. Include the scripts, asset versions, and runtime versions so I can reproduce the scenario. In this workflow, we expect Astra to do the following: Query the SimReady Search API to find relevant assets distributed on Hugging Face Reference/Payload them into an OpenUSD stage Generate Python code to assemble the workcell Configure the Pick-and-place task Render a preview for user review Figure 4. A robotic pick-and-place workcell assembled from SimReady assets illustrates how AI-assisted scene authoring can turn developer requirements into a simulation scenario for review and refinement in Isaac Sim. Compare AI factory layouts The same approach can support an ISV (independent software vendor) building an AI factory digital twin. The task shifts from robot interactions to equipment placement: arranging racks, cooling equipment, and supporting infrastructure within specified spatial constraints. Using SimReady assets from SimReady Central on Hugging Face, create two alternative AI factory layouts with racks and cooling equipment. Use the supplied equipment dimensions and aisle-clearance requirements. Check for equipment overlaps and clearance violations, and report any issues. Save each layout as an OpenUSD scene. Include the scene-building scripts, asset versions, and runtime versions so I can reproduce and compare the results. In this workflow, Astra would assemble the selected SimReady assets into two OpenUSD layouts, followed up by generating scripts to check equipment overlaps and aisle clearances against the supplied requirements. Developers could then inspect the layouts in their simulation application, compare equipment placement and access paths, and review any flagged issues before refining the preferred configuration. Figure 5. An AI factory layout assembled from SimReady assets illustrates how AI-assisted scene authoring supports equipment placement, aisle-clearance checks, and layout refinement in OpenUSD. In either example, developers can extend their environments in a few ways: Reuse the environment: Keep layout and task-specific changes in separate OpenUSD layers so the same source assets can support multiple experiments. Vary the scenarios: Introduce additional assets from the library and vary object placements, equipment configurations, or surrounding infrastructure to evaluate different conditions. Build application-specific tests: For robotics, configure training and evaluation tasks in Isaac Lab. For AI factories, connect the scene to the equipment data and simulation tools needed for analyses such as power distribution or cooling performance. Carry validated layouts into operations: For AI factories, connect the scene to live BMS and IT telemetry to keep the digital twin synchronized with an AI factory facility. Help shape the next wave of assets SimReady Central’s roadmap includes more OEM partners and a growing asset library, expanding the equipment and environments developers can assemble from reusable content. Community feedback will help identify which additions matter most. Tell us in the comments which assets you need, which runtimes you use, and where you encounter integration gaps. Submit OEM assets for inclusion in SimReady Central using the asset submission guide . OEM contributions can broaden the available content, while developer examples can show how assets work in different applications. Share examples of what you build in the comments and open an issue in SimReady Foundation for bugs or SimReady requirements feature requests. Use the resources below to find assets, build a scene, or contribute equipment models. Discover assets Find assets for your task: SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face Search with natural language: Describe the assets you need through the SimReady Central search endpoint powered by USD Search . Build your own asset browser: Explore the index-to-library skills in the SimReady Central GitHub repository . Build a scene Learn to assemble OpenUSD scenes: Follow the free OpenUSD learning path . Develop your robotics and digital twin skills: Explore the free physical AI courses . Build robotics simulations: Start with the Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab . Build AI factories: Start with an agent-assisted digital twin workflow . Prepare and contribute content Start the OEM contribution process: Follow the onboarding guide and find FAQ answers in the SimReady Central Library documentation . Choose the requirements for your asset: Review the profiles in SimReady Foundation . Prepare CAD models for simulation: Use the CAD-to-SimReady skills . Validate, package, and submit your assets: Follow the SimReady Central submission skill . Happy building, we can’t wait to see what you create! content: TechCrunch Founder Summit is a full-day gathering in Boston on November 4 where founders across all stages connect with top VCs and experienced entrepreneurs to gain tactical insights on building and scaling their companies. It’s the latest in our long line of founder-centric events, which are smaller and more hands-on than Disrupt. For the founder looking to really get in the weeds during a one-day crash course, Founder Summit is the ideal place to get a head start on your 2027 plans for everything from hiring, establishing product market fit, finding investors, improving your leadership skills, and more. Before you dig in on the event details, you can get info on all of our tickets, which are available for a $100 discount for investors and founders, right here . Even if you’re a student and an aspiring founder, or an investor looking to meet the next wave of East Coast innovators, we have an option for you. And those bringing a colleague get an even better reward, as for a limited time each pass comes with an additional free ticket via our BOGO sale . Who is TechCrunch Founder Summit for? All founders end up wrestling with the extensive, complicated mechanics of building a company from the ground up. There’s fundraising, hiring, legal, marketing, PR, and leadership, as well as the investors needing the means to vet, invest in, and develop founders as they build out their skills. Founder Summit is the best way to cover all of the challenging questions with community members who have been there, and lived to tell the tale, through constructive failure and massive success. When and where is TechCrunch Founder Summit? The event takes place on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, at the SoWa Power Station in Boston. It’s accessible via public transportation and a short walk from the Back Bay and Tufts Medical Center stops on the Orange Line, or the Broadway stop on the Red Line. Image Credits: TechCrunch / Getty Images What’s on the TechCrunch Founder Summit agenda? To deliver on that promise of equipping founders for success, this year’s agenda and speakers lean hard into fundraising, AI-native building, and leadership. Sessions include: Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself: Toast Co-founder and Director Steve Fredette shares his insights on keeping a company relevant amid evolving technologies and changing customer expectations. The Boston Founder Playbook : HqO co-founder and CEO Chase Garbarino on building a category-defining company outside Silicon Valley, having raised $200 million and scaled to 30+ countries. Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale : Bessemer Venture Partners ‘ Kent Bennett on validating demand and avoiding scaling before the fundamentals are in place. Built for AI From Day One : 7AI co-founder and CEO Lior Div on what changes when AI is the foundation of a company rather than a bolt-on feature. Not Every Dollar Is Equal : Cogent Security co-founder and CEO Vineet Edupuganti on evaluating investors and cap-table trade-offs beyond valuation. How to Spot the ‘King of the Hill’ Company : TDK Ventures investment director Tina Tosukhowong unpacking a framework for evaluating startups on economics, scalability, and timing. Your Pitch Has to Near the Next Conversation : TrueVentures Partner and Edisyl CEO Dave Balter instills the importance of making sure your pitch doesn’t just wow, but that it sparks a continued conversation throughout every minute of its delivery. Is there a pitch competition? We’re glad you asked! Founder Summit will once again feature the much-requested So You Think You Can Pitch? competition, during which three early stage startups will try to impress a panel of judges within four minutes each. Their approaches, and the judges’ feedback, is invaluable for improving your own pitches. Didn’t this event have a different name? Yes. Founder Summit was formerly known as Early Stage and All Stage . This year, we have the same mission, but with a new name. Keep that in mind if you want to do any more research before attending. Is TechCrunch Founder Summit just panels, or is there more to it? Founder Summit is far from a series of panels, though the agenda does provide a ton of valuable insights for founders and investors. In addition to all of those sessions, we also have our breakout sessions, where even more intimate panels discuss vital topics for the community to dive deeper into. There’s also networking available via the Braindate app to help connect investors with founders, or facilitate founders with similar challenges to bring their expertise together to reach shared solutions. Or that time is the perfect opportunity for students to build out their nascent network. Then there’s Founder Summit week, taking place November 1-7. That’s when all of our Side Events are held , expanding the opportunities for you to gather with the community. And if you’re especially eager to take part, you can apply to host your own Side Event right here . Image Credits: Halo Creative How much does a ticket cost, and how can I get the best price? Pricing moves in phases, with our next increase happened after October 16. Our current pricing tiers are Investor for $499, Founder for $299, and students for $149 . If you buy a second ticket for a co-founder or co-worker, you’ll also get an additional ticket for free. And bundles for groups for four or more offer additional discounts. Is there a free way to attend? Yes! We’re looking for volunteers to help staff the event, and those individuals will get a behind-the-scenes look at how the event comes together on top of their free access to programming beyond their shift. Learn more about our program, closed to new applicants October 19. Where can I register and learn more? You can get the full rundown of the event, with everything from up-to-date speaker information, the full agenda, logistics, and more right here . Ticket information across all three tiers is available here . And remember, our BOGO deal won’t last forever, act now before it expires . title: NVIDIA Kumo Forecast Combines Pretrained Time-Series Representations with Historical Pattern Retrieval and Interpretability
content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> NVIDIA Kumo Forecast Combines Pretrained Time-Series Representations with Historical Pattern Retrieval and Interpretability Enterprise + Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 5 Saira Qureshi sairaq Follow nvidia Aditi Gautam adgautam Follow nvidia Manikandan Ravikiran mravikirannvidia Follow nvidia Sena Ekiz neptunel1 Follow nvidia Viraj P Modak vmodak Follow nvidia :last-child]:mb-0"> Highlights (TL;DR) NVIDIA Kumo Forecast (formerly known as NV-Tesseract Forecasting) is a multi-variate time-series forecasting model that combines a pretrained Transformer backbone with Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR), a context-enhanced forecasting mode that blends direct model predictions with patterns retrieved from historical data. This includes interpretability of the results. Built on the MOMENT-1-large backbone, Kumo Forecast uses an approximately 340-million-parameter base encoder plus a trainable forecasting head. The library provides a DataFrame-first API, configurable forecast horizons, optional historical context for retrieval, and an interpretability framework that produces horizon-specific explanations without modifying the underlying forecaster. Kumo-Forecast is available under Apache 2.0 license . Model code: NVIDIA/Kumo-TS Model weights: nvidia/Kumo-Forecast The Shift to Context-Enhanced Time-Series Forecasting A forecasting system can draw on two different sources of information: representations learned during pretraining and historical observations available for the current application. Kumo-Forecast brings these together through a pretrained forecasting model and an optional retrieval pathway over historical context. In its direct forecasting path, Kumo-Forecast uses a MOMENT-based Transformer and a trained forecasting head to predict future values. In Domain Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR) mode, it also retrieves related patterns from historical data using a nearest-neighbor approach and combines that information with the direct forecast. This creates a distinction between the model’s input window and its retrieval context. The input window supplies recent observations for the forecast; a separate historical DataFrame can supply additional context for pattern retrieval. Developers can adjust how strongly the final prediction relies on each pathway through the library’s configuration options. Further information on DARR mode can be found in this published paper, Memory-Augmented Forecasting: Scalability and Generalization Across Temporal Domains How Kumo Forecast Works Kumo-Forecast combines four main components: a pretrained temporal encoder, a trainable forecasting head, historical-pattern retrieval mechanism and an interpretability framework. Pretrained Temporal Representations : The model uses the MOMENT-1-large Transformer encoder as its backbone. The architecture keeps encoder and embedder weights frozen while training the forecasting head, separating the pretrained representation model from the task-specific prediction layer. Direct Forecasting : The forecasting head maps the model’s representations to future values for the requested horizon. For horizons beyond the model’s native capability, there is support for autoregressive extension. This distinguishes a directly generated forecast from a longer forecast that extends predictions recursively. Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval : DARR augments direct forecasting with k-nearest-neighbor retrieval from historical context data. This process combines direct forecasts with historical-pattern retrieval, while the SDK accepts the historical context through a separate context_df argument. Interpretability : Kumo-Forecasting also includes a model-agnostic interpretability framework. When enabled, it produces an explanation bundle containing lag and feature attributions per forecast horizon, semantic-flow diagnostics, trajectory-stability diagnostics, and optional embedding Integrated Gradients.These outputs accompany the forecast rather than requiring a different forecasting architecture. Further details on interpretability can be found in this paper, NVExplain: Explaining Time Series Forecasting with Latent Trajectory Analysis and Structure-Preserving Surrogates Limitations Data must be numeric, temporal data. Supported input sequence lengths include 256, 512, 1024, and 2048 observations. Inputs consist of a timestamp column and one or more numeric value columns, represented as a pandas DataFrame or a CSV/JSON input. When leveraging DARR mode, the dimensions of the context must be similar to the context of the input. Demo: Predictive Maintenance The Factory Operations (FOX) Blueprint includes Early Access to the Predictive Maintenance module which leverages Kumo Anomaly and Kumo Forecast. It analyzes real-time data to predict future anomalies. Your browser does not support the video tag. Validate forecast quality across the intended horizons and operating conditions, consistent with NVIDIA’s requirement for use-case-specific testing Model code: NVIDIA/Kumo-TS Model weights: nvidia/Kumo-Forecast The Kumo-TS repository additionally provides an example for fine-tuning Kumo-Forecast on a user-supplied CSV. Developers therefore have both a pretrained inference workflow and a documented starting point for adapting the model to their own data. content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster Enterprise Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 23 +17 George Saon gsaon Follow ibm-granite Brian Kingsbury bedkingsbury Follow ibm-granite Ron Hoory rhoory Follow ibm-granite Vishal Sunder vishalsunder Follow ibm-granite Zvi Kons konszvi Follow ibm-granite Jeff Kuo ibm-jeffkuo Follow ibm-granite Samuel Thomas sthomas12 Follow ibm-granite Avihu Dekel Avihu Follow ibm-granite Hagai Aronowitz hagaia Follow ibm-granite Takashi Fukuda fukuda1 Follow ibm-granite Tohru Nagano tohru3 Follow ibm-granite Sashi Novitasari sasnov Follow ibm-granite Masayuki Suzuki szuk Follow ibm-granite Madison Lee kristunlee Follow ibm-granite :last-child]:mb-0"> We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, granite-speech-5.0-2b , and revised versions of two models the community already uses, granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus . Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said. Model Status What's new Best for granite-speech-5.0-2b New More accurate, noise- and reverb-robust automatic speech recognition (ASR), language-ID prompting, 2,000-term keyword biasing, better long-form translation High-accuracy multilingual transcription and translation granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc Updated Multilingual, native punctuation and capitalization, and more robust to noise and reverb High-throughput and on-device transcription granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus Updated Improved speaker attribution, timestamps, keyword biasing, and long-speech performance Meetings, calls, and other multi-speaker recordings Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control granite-speech-5.0-2b is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation. What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech: More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech. Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription. Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences. Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language. Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets. The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon. Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are official, as of 21 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets. Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster When we introduced Turbo CTC in August , it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most: Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese. Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step. More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings. It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level. Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale. Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when The updated granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas: Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall. Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review. Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%. Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists. Need raw speed or on-device transcription? Use granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc , and try it in the browser with our WebGPU streaming demo . Working with meetings or multi-speaker calls? Use granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus . These models are all released under an Apache 2.0 license with native support in Transformers. content: AI News Tech OpenAI says an AI agent lied about disabling its safety monitoring system Another OpenAI agent turned off automatic security alerts. Another OpenAI agent turned off automatic security alerts. by Emma Roth Oct 21, 2026, 1:57 PM UTC Image: The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. OpenAI disclosed a pair of safety incidents that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks. In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled its safety monitor when copying reference code — and then lied about it. “The reference didn’t configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user’s code,” Marcus Williams, an AI safety researcher at OpenAI, writes on X . “When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not.” A separate incident occurred after a GPT-6.1 Sol agent suppressed automatic security alerts to OpenAI’s security team on Slack. In this case, the AI agent carried over an earlier instruction not to send any Slack messages to OpenAI’s team, using that to justify turning off the alerts. Related Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu We’re running out of reasons to ignore AI safety These incidents add to security concerns surrounding AI agents, some of which have circumvented their testing environment’s restrictions to hack outside companies. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI says. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.
